newsitem.title: PERU: Japan asks for restraint at Peru hostage site.
newsitem.headline: Japan asks for restraint at Peru hostage site.

text.p: Japan asked Peru on Monday to limit police manoeuvres around the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima, fearing they could unsettle the 72 hostages held by Marxist rebels inside.
"I'm worrying how it may affect the hostages inside. I'm wondering if I can ask ... the Peruvian government not to go too far," Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told reporters in Tokyo.
"Not thinking of the hostages' mental state may have an adverse effect," he added.

In an apparent effort to unnerve the hostage takers inside the diplomatic mansion, police have thrown stones and garbage into the grounds, flown helicopters overhead and moved in armoured vehicles and men with high-powered rifles and night-vision equipment.
The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels have responded to the troop movements by firing shots into the air and defiantly shouting that they would not surrender.

Japanese Vice Foreign Minister Sadayuki Hayashi told a news conference Tokyo had conveyed its concern to Lima urging the government to pursue "earnest efforts toward a prompt conclusion of the hostage crisis."

The MRTA's international spokesman said the police activity indicated the government was preparing to storm the residence and warned that an attack would unleash a fierce backlash from the guerrilla movement.

"If the residence is stormed, the situation all across Peru will intensify and become much worse. All across Peru, armed commandos of the MRTA are ready to carry out attacks on economic and political targets," MRTA spokesman Isaac Velazco said in an inteview with Germany's junge Welt daily published on Monday.
"The deaths of Tupac Amaru fighters would escalate the conflict across the country," he added in the interview which was carried on the MRTA's Internet web page.

Until the spectacular assault on a lavish reception at the residence Dec. 17, President Alberto Fujimori had been credited with virtually wiping out the MRTA. Local analysts say less than 250 active members of the guerrilla group are still at large.
Fujimori, whose brother Pedro is among the captives, has said the police manoeuvres were not a buildup to an assault and insisted he was seeking a negotiated end to the standoff.
A mediator in the crisis said on Sunday he was hopeful the 41-day siege would be resolved peacefully.
"There is a small light on the horizon," said Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, a friend of Fujimori who has been accepted by both sides as a mediator.
Cipriani spoke to reporters hours after the rebels freed a police commander so that he could receive medical treatment.
Gen. Jose Rivas Rodriguez, a deputy chief in the Peruvian national police, was wheeled out of the residence on a stretcher and rushed to a nearby police hospital.
But the rebels quickly followed this gesture by singing their rebel hymn and pledging not to give up until their demands were met.
They sang again early on Monday in what has become a daily ritual of defiance. Following the singing, a rebel yelled "What is the objective of this mission? To win or to die!"
Talks remain deadlocked with the MRTA sticking to its main demand for the release of about 400 jailed comrades and the government refusing to even discuss it.
The roughly 15 guerrillas, armed with assault rifles and grenade launchers, originally seized more than 500 hostages but have freed most in what they called "goodwill gestures."

The remaining captives in the mined and booby-trapped house include two Peruvian ministers, congressmen, judges, police and army chiefs, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
